doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

title: Joining the Count Basie band and learning the Basie groove
summary: Funk experience did not hinder swinging; he locked in by listening to Bill Hughes, Mel Wanzo and Dennis Wilson.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Yeah. I remember looking at your sort of chronology and thinking after all those years of playing in funk bands did you have to sort of re-set when you got with Basie and like remember how to swing?
Oh no. I didn’t have to remember nothing.
That was still inside you, right?
Oh that music that locks into your body and you just hope the notes are right you know, because the Basie groove is a one time thing. It’s the best groove in the world I think.

I totally agree. There’s something about that rhythm section that just seemed like it was one instrument. They self-balanced themselves, they didn’t depend on a sound man to do that, it’s just like a phenomenon.

In fact Basie used to tell sound men, “Set it and forget it, go sit down somewhere, we will adjust among ourselves.” You know. In fact the whole band adjusted among themselves. They would play soft and they would play loud, and when they would play among themselves they would adjust the way it should be played you know. And somehow they all knew what to do or when to do it. You know?
As the new guy in the band you must have done a lot of observing to figure out how they were doing that?

Well the Count Basie band I kind of knew. I kind of knew what they were doing and how they were doing it. In fact the way I got to keep the Basie gig is because I listened to Bill © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Hughes, the bass trombone player. And he would kind of lead the band from the bottom. And Mel Wanzo wasn’t the best trombone player in the world but he could play that music the way it was supposed to be played. You know? And so I was listening to the two of them and the other two trombone players and we kind of locked together. You know Dennis Wilson, he was a perfectly well trained musician. He wrote arrangements with a ball point pen. Full band arrangements and he never made a mistake. And I just admired that so much you know. And I learned so much from them. And fell into that groove automatically without anybody telling me what to do you know.
